utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning, to all. I have with me here today my legal counsel, Mr. Peter Robinson, and I also have a Case Manager nearby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber convened this hearing to deliver its ruling on the accused's oral motion for a judgement of acquittal pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On the 11th of June, 2012, the accused moved for a judgement of acquittal on each of the 11 counts in the indictment. The Prosecution respond on 13th of June, 2012, opposing the motion. The Chamber will start by recalling the applicable legal standard. Rule 98 bis as amended in 2004 provides that at the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall, by oral decision, and after hearing the oral submission of the parties, enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there's no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. As enunciated in numerous 98 bis decisions, including the cases against Mrksic et al., Popovic et al., and Milutinovic, et al., the test to be applied is whether there's evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the particular accused on the count in question. The test is not whether a Trial Chamber would convict beyond reasonable doubt but, rather, whether it could do so. Therefore, where there is no evidence to sustain a count or where the only relevant evidence is so incapable of belief that it could not properly sustain a conviction even when the evidence is taken at its highest for the Prosecution, a judgement of acquittal will be entered with respect to that count. At this stage, the Trial Chamber is not to evaluate the credibility of witnesses or the strengths and weaknesses of contradictory evidence. Furthermore, a ruling now that there is evidence capable of sustaining a conviction on a particular count does not mean that the Trial Chamber will enter a conviction at the end of the case. The Chamber also notes that where evidence is mentioned later in support of its findings, the fact that it has been considered for the purpose of this ruling is no fixed indication that the Chamber will ultimately accept it in whole or in part. Similarly, the fact that certain evidence is not mentioned in the Rule 98 bis rulings does not mean that the Chamber may not accept it and rely upon it in its final judgement. The Rule also does not require that the Chamber be satisfied that there's evidence supporting each of the individual charges making up a specific count. For instance, for persecutions under Count 3, it is sufficient that there be evidence on one or several forms of persecutions alleged. It is also sufficient if there is evidence capable of supporting a conviction on the basis of one of the modes of responsibility charged in the indictment. Although the accused has challenged all of the modes of responsibility, this decision concentrates on assessing the responsibility of the accused on each of the 11 counts for commission under Article 7(1) of the Tribunal's Statute through his participation in the four alleged joint criminal enterprises. Only if there were no evidence under this mode of responsibility would the Chamber turn to the other modes under Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. The Chamber wishes to make two preliminary notes. First, with regard to the accused's challenge in relation to the overly broad use of the term "Bosnian Serb forces," the Chamber recalls paragraph 32 of the decision on two motions alleging defects in the form of the indictment issued by the Pre-trial Chamber in this case on the 12th of May, 2009, in which it found that the indictment was not defective in regard to the specificity of pleading the identity of the alleged members of the joint criminal enterprises and the physical perpetrators. The Chamber further notes that throughout this ruling it will use the term "Bosnian Serb forces" as defined by the Prosecution in paragraph 14(b) of the indictment. Second, the Chamber notes that for the purpose of this ruling, it will use the term of "municipalities" as defined by the Prosecution in paragraph 48 of the indictment. The Chamber will present its ruling first in relation to the hostages component of the case before turning to the Sarajevo component, then the Srebrenica component, and finally concluding with the municipalities component. The Chamber now turns to the accused's challenges in relation to the hostages component of the case. As part of his challenges, the accused submits that the detained UN personnel were combatants taking part in the hostilities and that Article 3 of the Statute encompasses protections guaranteed by Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and thus only protects persons who were taking no active part in hostilities. In relation to his mens rea, he further submits that he considered at the time of their detention that the UN personnel were being detained as prisoners of war. The Prosecution responds that the status of UN personnel is irrelevant because Common Article 3 protects persons taking no active part in hostilities, including members of the armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed "hors de combat" by their detention. The Prosecution further responds that any statements by the accused that the detained UN personnel were prisoners of war is contradicted by evidence showing his intent to gain an advantage or obtain a concession as a direct consequence of their detention. The Chamber will not determine at this stage what constitutes the legal elements of the time of hostage-taking under the Statute. However, the Chamber recalls that the Appeals Chamber in this case, in its decision on appeal of Trial Chamber's decision on preliminary motion to dismiss Count 11 of the indictment issued on the 9th of July, 2009, held that Common Article 3 prohibits hostage-taking of any person taking no active part in the hostilities, including those placed "hors de combat" by detention. It is therefore sufficient to note that even if the UN personnel were combatants immediately before their detention, they were rendered "hors de combat" by virtue of their detention and thus were entitled to the minimum protections guaranteed by Common Article 3. The Chamber received evidence from Patrick Rechner, Joseph Gelissen, and Marcus Helgers, who were UN personnel in 1995 detained by the Bosnian Serb forces and placed in areas of military significance for the Army of Republika Srpska, also known as the VRS. They were threatened with death unless NATO stopped their air-strikes against Bosnian Serb military targets. The Chamber also heard evidence from Rechner, Helgers, and Rupert Smith that the threats were communicated both to the detained UN personnel directly, as well as to Smith and the headquarters of the United Nations Protection Force, also known as UNPROFOR. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that there's evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the crime of taking hostages as a violation of the laws or customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute and specifically Common Article 3 was carried out by Bosnian Serb forces between May and June 1995. Turning now to the accused's responsibility under Count 11, the Chamber heard evidence from Smith and has admitted documents such as P2137, P2149, P2268, and P5013, all of which indicate that following the NATO air-strikes, the Bosnian Serb political leadership and the VRS enacted a plan to detain UN personnel and place them in locations of military significance for the VRS. The objective of this plan was to stop NATO from continuing further air-strikes as shown by the threats made to the UN that the detained personnel would be killed if another air-strike occurred. The same evidence also indicates that the members of the Bosnian Serb political leadership and military who participated in this plan included the accused and Ratko Mladic. Accordingly, the Chamber is satisfied that there is evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could find beyond reasonable doubt that there existed a joint criminal enterprise, the common purpose of which was to take UN personnel hostage in order to compel NATO to abstain from conducting further air-strikes against Bosnian Serb military targets and which involved a plurality of persons, including the accused. In relation to the accused's contribution specifically, the Chamber received evidence that by virtue of his position as the Supreme Commander of the VRS and president of the Republika Srpska, he approved orders issued by the VRS to detain UN personnel. These are P2137 and P5026. The Chamber also heard from Smith that prior to the detention of UN personnel, the accused told him that if NATO were to conduct air-strikes against Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs would treat the UN as their enemy and would attack or detain UN personnel. This is confirmed by P2264 and P2265. The Chamber also received evidence indicating that the accused shared the intent to take the UN personnel hostage. For example, as can be seen from P2137, the accused approved an order on the 27th of May, 1995, directing the VRS to place UN personnel in locations of potential targets for the NATO air-strikes. On the 29th of May, 1995, the accused, in a telephone conversation which included Krajisnik, stated that his demand as a condition for the release of the UN personnel was -- that his demand as a condition for the release of the UN personnel was that there would be no more NATO air-strikes. This is P5626. Later, on the 15th of June, 1995, at the 51st Session of the RS Assembly, the accused stated that the Bosnian Serbs had released most of the UN personnel except for the 15 people who were still being detained for the purpose of trying to keep the VRS weapons in Sarajevo and added that, "We even somewhat benefited from this whole crisis." This is Exhibit P1410. Accordingly, the Chamber is satisfied that there's evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could find beyond reasonable doubt that the accused voluntarily participated in a joint criminal enterprise, the common purpose of which was to take UN personnel hostage in order to compel NATO to abstain from conducting further air-strikes against Bosnian Serb military targets. There is also evidence to suggest that he shared the intent of the other members of this joint criminal enterprise to carry out its objective. The Chamber will now deal with the accused's challenges as they concern the Sarajevo component of the case. In relation to Count 5 and 6, the accused submits that there is no evidence of his mens rea in terms of planning, aiding, abetting, instigating, and committing murders. Because the accused also submits in relation to his challenges to Counts 9 and 10 that there is no evidence that any sniping or shelling incident was committed from the Serb side, the Chamber understands his challenge to also cover the actus reus of murders alleged to have occurred in Sarajevo. The Prosecution responds that evidence shows that civilians in Sarajevo were frequently targeted by Bosnian Serb fire. The Chamber will first address the issue of whether there's evidence that murders occurred in Sarajevo and were committed by Bosnian Serb forces. The Chamber has received a large body of evidence going to the killings that took place in Sarajevo, as well as to the fact that these were committed by Bosnian Serb forces. For example, Bakir Nakas, Fatima Zaimovic, and Dragan Miokovic testified generally about a large number of persons killed in Sarajevo as a result of the shelling and sniping in the city. In addition, there is also testimonial and documentary evidence relating to a number of scheduled shelling and sniping incidents which resulted in deaths and which were said to have been committed by Bosnian Serb forces. As an example, in relation to scheduled shelling incident G6 where a number of children died as a result of shelling while playing football in Dobrinja, the Chamber received not only testimonial evidence but also evidence in the form of investigative reports prepared at the time by the BiH Ministry of Internal Affairs, also known as BiH MUP, as well as by UNPROFOR, all pointing to the Bosnian Serb forces as the perpetrators. The Chamber refers here to P1443 and P1698. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that there's evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that murder charged as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 5(a) of the Statute and as a violation of the laws or customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute and specifically Common Article 3 were carried out by Bosnian Serb forces in Sarajevo. In relation to Counts 9 and 10, the accused submits that there's no evidence of the existence of a siege in Sarajevo but rather the Bosnian Serbs conducted a military policy of "containing" the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, also known as ABiH. He also submits that there's no evidence of terror in Sarajevo or that any sniping or shelling incident was committed from the Serb side or that the Serb side fired indiscriminately. Finally, he claims that there is no evidence that Sarajevo was a civilian zone or that it was the target of any militarily unjustified action by the Serb side. In response, the Prosecution refers to numerous witnesses who have testified that the campaign of shelling and sniping conducted by Bosnian Serb forces was intended to inflict terror on the civilian population, that the fire directed against Sarajevo was indiscriminate, and that it was directed primarily at the civilian population. The Chamber notes that a number of witnesses testified that the city of Sarajevo, together with its civilians, was in fact encircled or besieged by Bosnian Serb forces and not just contained for a military purpose. The Chamber refers here to the testimony of Colm Doyle, Jeremy Bowen, and Richard Mole, as well as to D235. These witnesses, in addition to Anthony Banbury, Pyers Tucker, David Harland and Herbert Okun also testified that, while besieged, the city was constantly shelled and sniped by the Bosnian Serb forces using indiscriminate and disproportionate fire with the intent to terrorise the civilian population, including women and children. Indeed, many witnesses used the term "terror" during their testimony. The Chamber has also been provided with both testimonial evidence, such as the evidence of Ekrem Suljevic, Milomir Soja, and Harry Konings and documentary evidence such as P1201 and P1310, going to the use by the Bosnian Serb forces of highly inaccurate and highly destructive modified air-bombs. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that there is evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the crimes of terror and unlawful attacks charged under Article 3 of the Statute were carried out by Bosnian Serb forces in Sarajevo. The Chamber now turns to the accused's responsibility for Counts, 5, 6, 9, and 10, still in relation to Sarajevo. Some of his challenges mentioned earlier such as his submission that there was no terror in Sarajevo or that he had no mens rea to commit murders also pertained to his responsibility. In addition to those challenges, he submits that there was no motive for the Serbs to terrorise the population in Sarajevo as the Serbs were not seeking to capture the territory in and around it. The Prosecution responds that these assertions are directly contradicted by the weight of the evidence. First, the Chamber has heard from a number of witnesses, including Harland, KDZ088, and Okun that the Bosnian Serb military and political leadership, including the accused, Krajisnik, Biljana Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic, Mladic, and Stanislav Galic were in general united in their position when it came to Sarajevo. For example, Okun testified that one of the Serb goals was the division of Sarajevo into Serb and Muslim parts and that this was the constant refrain of Bosnian Serb leadership during the peace negotiations. Second, the Chamber recalls the evidence briefly referred to earlier in relation to the campaign of sniping and shelling in Sarajevo as charged under Count 9. In addition, and with respect to the accused's challenge that Bosnian Serbs had no know motive to terrorise the city, the Chamber has heard from a number of witnesses such as Doyle, Mole, Michael Rose, and Harland contradicting that assertion. For example, Harland testified that the overall strategy of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and in particular that of the accused, was to modulate the level of suffering in Sarajevo as it suited his political goals, increasing it to force the Bosnian Muslims to accept peace deals on Serb terms and preserve territorial status quo, or reducing it in the face of threats of international military intervention. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that there's evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that between April 1992 and November 1995, there was a joint criminal enterprise to establish and carry out a campaign of sniping and shelling against the civilian population of Sarajevo. There is also evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the objective of this joint criminal enterprise involved the commission of crimes of terror, unlawful attacks on civilians, and murder. With respect to his own contribution to the events in Sarajevo, the accused submits that there's no evidence that he had anything but a positive attitude on the delivery of humanitarian aid to the city. He also mentioned difficulties in controlling a popular army consisting of soldiers who were locals and former residents of Sarajevo. The Prosecution responds that these assertions are directly contradicted by the weight of the evidence and that on the contrary, the very nature of the campaign against the city shows that the accused was in overall control over the shelling, the sniping, and the terror. The Chamber has heard extensive evidence about the accused being both the president of the Republika Srpska and the Supreme Commander of the VRS, as shown by P3036, which gave him broad de jure and de facto powers over those forces, including the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, also known as the SRK, and which ensured his presence at various negotiations relating to Sarajevo. The Chamber also heard ample evidence about the accused's involvement in the events in Sarajevo as alleged in paragraphs 14 and 19 of the indictment. For example, the Chamber heard that during his speech at the 16th Assembly Session of the Serbian Republic of BiH of 12th of May, 1992, the accused explained, with respect to Sarajevo, that, "The battle in Sarajevo and for Sarajevo, seen strategically and tactically, is of decisive importance because it does not allow the establishment of even the illusion of a state," and stated that, "Alija does not have a state while we have a part of Sarajevo." The accused also stated that "the fighting in Sarajevo keeps the fighting far away from all those areas where we could possibly have conflicts with Muslims," noting also that, as the Bosnian Serbs expected, "if there's a war, it would start in Sarajevo and end in Sarajevo. " These are quotes from P956. Harland testified that in line with the Serb leadership's strategy to terrorise the city for political gains, the accused told him that it would not be politically useful to force the city to surrender as this would prompt a Western military response. The Chamber also notes here the evidence of KDZ088. In relation to the accused's challenge that it was difficult to control a popular army of soldiers who were Sarajevo locals, the Chamber has heard evidence to the effect that the accused was in complete de jure and de facto control over the VRS. The Chamber refers to D325 and the testimony of John Wilson, Harland, and Rose. Also, Okun testified that the accused said to him in September 1992 that the VRS had a unified command and that he had full power over it, including over 95 per cent of the irregulars. The Chamber also heard evidence from Okun, Wilson, and Harland that the accused justified the activities of the Bosnian Serbs in Sarajevo, stating that they were conducted in self-defence or in response to provocation by the Bosnian Muslims. Harland also added that during their meetings the accused would be presented with information about specific shelling or sniping incidents but would normally deny that there was a problem or would say that he would look into it or that he had already issued orders that the firing should stop. According to Harland, such promises by the accused had very little effect. Contrary to the accused's submission, the Chamber also heard evidence from Harland, Smith, and Rose about the accused directing and/or authorising the restriction of humanitarian aid to Sarajevo. Harland testified that the accused would use eight levers of pressure on Sarajevo, one of which was the control over humanitarian supplies, and would often stop the supplies from coming into the city when there was no threat of a NATO intervention. Harland also testified that on 26th of July, 1994, the accused decided to close two of the Blue Routes used to deliver humanitarian aid and that, on the 8th of April, 1995, he decided to close Sarajevo altogether by halting the Sarajevo air-lift. Accordingly, the Chamber is of the view that there is evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the accused voluntarily participated in the joint criminal enterprise relating to Sarajevo through both his acts and omissions and that he shared the intent of the other members of this joint criminal enterprise to carry out its objective, namely to establish and carry out a campaign of sniping and shelling against the civilian population of Sarajevo with the incident of spreading terror. There is also evidence to suggest that he shared the intent of the other members of the joint criminal enterprise to commit the crimes of murder, terror, and unlawful attacks on civilians. The Chamber will now deal with the accused's challenges regarding the Srebrenica component of the case. In relation to Counts 4, 5, and 6 in Srebrenica, the accused submits that there is no evidence that civilians were killed and makes a number of challenges to specify killing incidents. The Prosecution responds citing evidence to the contrary. The Chamber has received a considerable body of evidence suggesting that a substantial number of unarmed Bosnian Muslims were killed in Srebrenica by Bosnian Serb forces during the period alleged in the indictment. The Chamber refers, for example, to KDZ039 and KDZ064 in relation to Orahovac; to KDZ066 in relation to Cerska Valley; to KDZ084 in relation to Sandici; and to Ahmo Hasic and Drazen Erdemovic in relation to Branjevo Farm. Additionally, the Chamber heard evidence from KDZ063 and KDZ071 in relation to the killing on the 13th of July, 1995, of hundreds of Muslim men in a warehouse in Kravica, which goes against the accused's challenge as to why the Kravica incident occurred. Furthermore, the Chamber heard evidence from KDZ065 in relation to the killing on the 13th of July, 1995, of Bosnian Muslim men at the bank of the Jadar River, which goes against the accused's challenge that there is no evidence proving killings before the Kravica incident. The Chamber also heard evidence from Johannes Rutten and Paul Groenewegen in relation to killings in Potocari on or about 12th and 13th of July, 1995, which goes against the accused's challenge that there were no killings in places where there was a greater military or police presence, such as in Potocari. The Chamber also received extensive evidence regarding the presence of Bosnian Serb forces in the Srebrenica area which were involved in the alleged commission of crimes against Bosnian Muslims. For example, the Chamber received evidence from KDZ064, KDZ084, Dragan Jovic, Srecko Acimovic, Mevludin Oric, and Erdemovic on the presence of, inter alia, security officers from various VRS units and members of the RS MUP, the 10th Sabotage detachment, and the Zvornik Brigade's 2nd and 4th Battalions at various execution sites. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that there's evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that murder charged as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 5(a) of the Statute and as a violation of the laws or customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute and specifically Common Article 3 and extermination charged as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 5(b) of the Statute were carried out by Bosnian Serb forces in the Srebrenica area in 1995. The Chamber will now turn to the accused's challenges in relation to Counts 7 and 8 insofar as they relate to Srebrenica. The accused submits that there was no planned deportation but that by the 11th of July, 1995, the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica wanted to be evacuated and conveyed that request to Mladic and the UN. The Prosecution submits on the contrary that there was a clear intent by the accused and the VRS to forcibly displace the population and that the desperate conditions imposed by them on the enclave were intended to make life unbearable in the months leading up to the attack, contributing to the population's lack of any other choice but to leave the enclave. The Chamber notes that it will not make a determination at this stage as to what constitutes a de facto or de jure border for the purposes of deportation. The Chamber heard evidence from Joseph Kingori, Rutten, and Robert Franken that when the Srebrenica enclave fell to Bosnian Serb forces, the Bosnian Muslim population had no other choice but to leave Srebrenica town and move to Potocari. Kingori and Christine Schmidtz both testified about the dire humanitarian situation faced by approximately 20.000 refugees in Potocari due to the lack of food and medical supplies. The Chamber also received evidence from various witnesses, including KDZ070, KDZ186, and Rutten about the forcible displacement of thousands of Bosnian Muslim women, children, and elderly men from Potocari in July 1995, when they were ordered by the VRS soldiers to board buses. The Chamber also heard from Kingori and Mile Janjic that the forcible displacement of population from Srebrenica was planned by the VRS. There is also testimonial documentary evidence such as the evidence of Kingori and P1385, suggesting that the goal of the Bosnian Serb leadership in organising the forcible displacement was to permanently remove the Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica. The intent of Bosnian Serb forces to forcibly displace the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica is shown by the organisation of the transportation for the refugees in Potocari and the systematic nature in which the women, children, and some elderly men were separated from the military-aged men and taken towards Bosnian Muslim held territory as shown, for example, by the testimony of KDZ070, Hasic, Groenewegen, and Evert Albert Rave, and by P4935 and P4464. Further evidence supporting the intent to forcibly displace this population is shown in P4075, a Bratunac Brigade report of the 4th of July, 1995, setting forth the goal for the civilian population of Srebrenica that "their life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible, so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." Accordingly, the Chamber is satisfied that there is evidence upon which, if accepted, the reasonable trier of fact could find beyond reasonable doubt that the crimes of deportation and forcible transfer, an inhumane act, as crimes against humanity and charged under Articles 5(d) and 5(i) of the Statute were carried out by Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica in July 1995. The accused does not raise any specific challenges to Count 3 with respect to Srebrenica, although some of the submissions he made in relation to the killings and the forcible displacement of the population from Srebrenica could also be considered as challenges to Count 3. The evidence before the Chamber in relation to forcible displacement and killings in and around Srebrenica in 1995, as already addressed earlier, suggests that the events occurred according to a persecutory pattern of behaviour. This pattern can first be inferred from the evidence on the number of Bosnian Muslim victims killed in Srebrenica, as evidenced by, among others, the testimony of Ewa Tabeau, and Dusan Janc, as well as by the number of victims transferred to Bosnian Muslim held territory and the organised way in which the forcible displacement was carried out in a short period of time. Furthermore, the Chamber heard evidence suggesting that Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica were killed on the basis of their ethnic and religious affiliation, thus indicating that the killings were therefore carried out with the requisite persecutory intend by the Bosnian Serb forces. Similarly, in relation to the specific intent required for the forcible displacement of people out of Potocari to constitute persecutions, the Chamber has received evidence suggesting that Bosnian Muslims were subject to forcible displacement on the basis of their ethnic and religious affiliation. Therefore, the perpetrators acted with the requisite specific intent to discriminate on political, racial, or religious grounds. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that there's evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the persecutions charged as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 5(h) of the Statute were committed in Srebrenica in July and August 1995 by Bosnian Serb forces against Bosnian Muslims with the intent to discriminate against them specifically based on political, racial, or religious grounds. The Chamber now turns to the accused's challenges in relation to Count 2, genocide, Srebrenica. In addition to the accused's challenges to the killings per se, which have already been dealt with earlier, the accused submits that there's no evidence on the perpetrators' intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica. As discussed earlier in relation to Counts 4, 5, and 6, there's evidence before the Chamber that the military-aged Bosnian Muslim men in Srebrenica were the target of large-scale killings. This indicates that the part of targeted group within the meaning of Article 4 of the Statute was indeed the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica as part of Bosnian Muslims -- as part of the "Bosnian Muslim national, ethnical and/or religious group as such" as alleged in paragraph 41 of the indictment. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that there is evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica were targeted for destruction. In relation to the accused's challenge as to the lack of genocidal intent of the physical perpetrators of the killings in Srebrenica, the Chamber recalls that the specific intent of such perpetrators by its nature is not usually susceptible to direct proof but can be inferred from various factors, including the general context of the case, the numerical size of the atrocities committed, the repetition of destructive and discriminatory attacks, or the existence of a plan or policy to commit the underlying offence. In this respect, the Chamber refers to the Jelisic and Krstic Appeal Judgement. First, the evidence before the Chamber on the scheduled incidents as a whole suggests that killings were organised on a large scale, similarly to a military operation. In addition to the extensive evidence before the Chamber on the presence of various VRS and MUP units in Srebrenica, as discussed in relation to Counts 4, 5, and 6, the Chamber also received evidence, including from Milenko Katanic, on the assistance of local authorities in the burial of bodies after the mass executions. Accordingly, the evidence before the Chamber on the number of victims killed as well as on the facts that only Bosnian Muslim men and boys were targeted for summary executions and that the Bosnian Serb forces tried to kill each and every able-bodied Bosnian Muslim man in Srebrenica suggests the systematic nature and scale of the crimes committed, as well as the systematic targeting of the group. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that there is evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that genocide charged pursuant to Article 4 of the Statute was carried out by Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica. The Chamber now turns to the accused's responsibility for Counts 2 to 8 inclusive still in relation to Srebrenica. The accused submits that the combat activities in Srebrenica had a legitimate military purpose, that the question of the VRS entering Srebrenica only became relevant on the night of 10th of July, 1995, and that the VRS only entered Srebrenica once the town was abandoned by the 28th ABiH division and the civilian population. The Prosecution submits on the contrary, that the operation to take Srebrenica was a culmination of the accused's efforts to ethnically cleanse Eastern Bosnia and refers to evidence showing contact by the VRS with civilians in Srebrenica town on the 11th of July, 1995. First, the Chamber heard evidence that as early as 1992 and continuing until the 11th of July, 1995, the Bosnian Serb leadership implemented a policy which resulted in the large-scale expulsion of the non-Serb population from Bosnian-Serb claimed territories in BiH, and specifically in the permanent removal of Bosnian Muslim populations in Srebrenica. This policy was first formulated by the accused in May 1992 through the six strategic goals and following the creation of the VRS and the appointment of Mladic as the commander of the VRS Main Staff, implemented through the issuance of a number of successive operational directives, as well as by the issuance by the Drina Corps of order Krivaja 95 on the 2nd of July, 1995, which culminated in the attack on the Srebrenica enclave a few days later. The documentary evidence before the Chamber in support of this policy includes P781, P838, P961, P976, P2246, and P4481. There is also evidence suggesting that the accused approved the Srebrenica operation, as illustrated by his own statement at the 52nd and the 54th Sessions of the Republika Srpska Assembly in August and October 1995, as well as during a television interview. These are P1412, P1415, and P4555. The Chamber also heard evidence indicating that as the Srebrenica enclave fell, the Bosnian Serb leadership implemented a policy to eliminate the Bosnian Muslim population in Srebrenica. There is evidence that shows that the heavy VRS offensive, as shown in documents P4143 and P4147, led to the fall of Srebrenica town on the 11th of July, 1995. Video footage taken at the time shows that once Srebrenica town was taken, Mladic, Zivanovic, Radislav Krstic, Vujadin Popovic, Vinko Pandurevic and other Bosnian Serb forces advanced onwards towards Potocari, where part of the civilians had fled, and then towards Bratunac. This is P4201. The Chamber also refers to P2992. Contrary to the accused's submission that the VRS only entered Srebrenica town once it was abandoned by the civilian population and the ABiH 28th Division, the Chamber heard evidence from Erdemovic, a member of the VRS 10th Sabotage Detachment, that his unit established contact with the Bosnian Muslim population, including some elderly people and a military-aged man upon his surrender in the centre of Srebrenica town on the 11th of July, 1995. The Chamber received evidence from Kingori as well as from P4935 and the video footage admitted as P4201 on the meetings held at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac on the 11th and 12th of July, 1995, with DutchBat officials, Mladic, and other members of the Bosnian Serb forces. This evidence indicates that during these meetings Mladic told the Bosnian Muslim civilian representatives "you can either all leave, all stay, or all die here." Mladic also told them to bring the people who can secure the surrender of weapons and save their people from destruction. The evidence before the Chamber discussed earlier in relation to Counts 2 through 8 shows the separation of Bosnian Muslim men of military age from the Bosnian Muslim women, children, and elderly men by the VRS. Bosnian Muslim women, children, and some elderly men were subjected to forcible displacement, while the military-aged men were taken to various locations and executed. The evidence cited previously in relation to Counts 2 to 8 inclusive also shows the organised and systematic manner in which the VRS acted to implement the policy to eliminate the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica. Accordingly, the Chamber is satisfied that there is evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that there existed a joint criminal enterprise composed of members of the VRS, MUP, and the Bosnian Serb leadership, including the accused, the purpose of which was to eliminate the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica. With respect to his own contribution to the events in Srebrenica, the accused submits that there is no evidence that he planned, instigated, ordered and/or aided and abetted genocide in Srebrenica, nor as to who made the decision on the genocide and the killings in general. The accused adds that he could not and did not have knowledge of what was happening on the ground both in relation to the killings or the forcible displacement in Srebrenica. The Prosecution responds that, on the contrary, the accused was constantly kept abreast by the VRS, the MUP, and the civilian authorities of developments on the ground and that he knew of the forcible displacement and the killings as they were happening. As stated earlier, the Chamber has heard ample evidence, including testimony of Milovanovic and Skrbic, and as shown by P3036, about the accused's role as president of the Republika Srpska and Supreme Commander of the VRS which gave him broad de jure and de facto powers over those forces, including all the VRS units deployed in Srebrenica. This is confirmed by the accused's own statements during the 39th Session of the RS Assembly that: "I am the one who signs, who decides, and I will be responsible for each decision." This is P1388. The Chamber also heard ample evidence about the accused's involvement in the events in Srebrenica as alleged in paragraphs 14 and 24 of the indictment. Contrary to his challenge that he did not and could not have had knowledge of what was happening on the ground during the Srebrenica operation, the Chamber received evidence on the flow of communication up and down the chains of command in the VRS, the police, and the State Security Service, as well as between different reporting entities. The Chamber refers, inter alia, to the evidence of Christian Nielsen and to P2984, P2996, P4450, P4932, and D2099. Generally, in relation to information coming from the VRS, there is documentary evidence showing that daily reports were sent to the accused by the Main Staff, at least from 12th to 14th of July, 1995. These are P3054, P4457, and P4464. In addition, the Chamber heard evidence from Slavica Ristic, Tomislav Premovic, and Robert Djurdjevic on the accused's direct communication with Mladic on the 13th and 14th of July, 1995, regarding the Srebrenica operation. The evidence also indicates that the accused was receiving information from the MUP as exemplified by the meetings between the accused and Tomo Kovac on the 13th, 14th, 15th, and 18th of July, 1995, and by the fact that Kovac was receiving intelligence information reports from the field. The Chamber refers to P2242, P2987, P4932, P4933, and P5137. The Chamber also heard evidence from Katanic that Miroslav Deronjic communicated by telephone almost daily with the accused during the Srebrenica operation as confirmed by their conversation on the 13th of July, 1995, in which Deronjic reported to the accused about approximately 2.000 Bosnian Muslims from Potocari who were transported and detained in Bratunac. This is P4618. The accused also met with Deronjic on the 14th of July, 1995, as indicated by P2242, P4382, and Djurdjevic's evidence. In relation to the accused's challenge as to his knowledge of the killings in Srebrenica, the Chamber heard evidence, including that of KDZ122, that members of the VRS chain of command were aware of orders to kill the Bosnian Muslim men from Srebrenica. The Chamber also heard evidence from Katanic about a meeting between Deronjic and the accused where Deronjic allegedly reported on the killings in Kravica on the 13th of July, 1995. As for the accused's submission that there's no evidence that he knew or contributed to any deportation in Srebrenica, the Chamber refers to documentary evidence indicating that the accused was being informed by the VRS Main Staff as early as 12th of July, 1995, of the organised transport of about 10.000 Bosnian Muslims from Potocari towards Kladanj. The Chamber here refers to P166, P3054, P4388, and P4464. The Chamber has also heard evidence of the accused's encouragement of the VRS involved in the Srebrenica operation. Specifically, the Chamber received documentary evidence such as P1412, P4501, P4555, and P5121, as well as the testimony of Skrbic, Djurdjevic, and Premovic in relation to the promotion of Krstic on the 13th of July, 1995, to corps commander of the Drina Corps, immediately after the fall of Srebrenica, as a result of his direct involvement in the planning of the taking over of the Srebrenica enclave. As discussed earlier, the Chamber has heard evidence indicating that genocidal acts took place in the Srebrenica area in the summer of 1995 and that they were committed with the requisite specific intent for genocide. In light of all the evidence presented, the Chamber is of the view that the accused's genocidal intent may be inferred from the evidence received on the systematic nature and scale of the crimes committed in Srebrenica, as well as from the evidence on the targeting of the specific group of Bosnian Muslims and the accused's acts and omissions in relation to the events that took place there in 1995, as discussed earlier. Accordingly, the Chamber is of the view that there is evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the accused voluntarily participated in a joint criminal enterprise, the common purpose of which was to eliminate the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica through the commission of the crimes as charged in paragraph 20 of the indictment. There is also evidence to suggest that the accused shared the intent of the other members of this joint criminal enterprise to carry out its objectives, including the specific intent to commit genocide and the specific intent to discriminate against the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica specifically based on political, racial, or religious grounds. Before we turn to the municipalities component, given the timing, the Chamber will take a break for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will now turn to the municipalities component of the case. In relation to Count 3, the accused submits that there is no evidence that events occurred in the municipalities according to a pattern of behaviour. The Prosecution does not respond directly to this specific challenge by the accused but refers as an example to the active destruction of virtually all the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat religious sites in the municipalities. The Chamber has received extensive evidence about a pattern of persecutions through killings, deportations, and destruction of cultural and religious symbols committed across the municipalities by Bosnian Serb forces against the Bosnian Muslim and/or Bosnian Croat population. For example, in relation to Drina valley and the Prijedor area, Harland testified that: "You would sometimes find hundreds and hundreds of houses blown up, burnt out, or destroyed, and then one house would not be destroyed in the middle, would have little garden or something, and then they would have written on it in big paint 'Srpska Kuca,' meaning this is a Serbian house, indicating that huge numbers of the non-Serb population had been violently expelled." On this topic, the Chamber also refers to the evidence of KDZ240. The accused also submits that there is no evidence of forcible transfer or deportation as acts of persecutions in the municipalities. However, the Chamber has received extensive evidence that a large number of Bosnian Muslim and/or Bosnian Croats from the municipalities were intentionally forcibly displaced either within or across a de jure or a de facto border by Bosnian Serb forces. The Chamber refers here to the evidence of Asim Egrlic, KDZ011, and KDZ605. In addition, the accused submits that there is no evidence that people were detained on the basis of their ethnic affiliation but argues that they were detained for the purpose of investigations. He also claims that there is no evidence of forced labour in the municipalities and refers instead to evidence showing that work was voluntary. However, the Chamber notes that it has received evidence about Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, including women and children, being detained in the municipalities, specifically on the basis of their ethnic affiliation and not solely for the purposes of investigation. The Chamber here refers to the testimony of KDZ051, KDZ239, and KDZ240. The Chamber has also received evidence from a number of witnesses, including KDZ024, KDZ051, and KDZ610, about instances of Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat detainees being forced by Bosnian Serb forces to work, including digging graves and trenches in detention facilities. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that there is evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that during the period relevant to the indictment in the municipalities, Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats were detained specifically on the basis of their ethnic affiliation, that forced labour was imposed on Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats by Bosnian Serb forces, and that Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats were forcibly displaced either within or across a de jure or a de facto border with the specific intent to discriminate against them on political, racial, or religious grounds. In addition to the evidence discussed earlier, the Chamber received extensive evidence supporting Count 3 in the municipalities as charged in the indictment. This includes the testimony of KDZ024 relating to Kljuc; KDZ048 relating to Prijedor; KDZ239 relating to Foca; KDZ610 relating to Zvornik; Hajrudin Karic relating to Pale; KDZ240 relating to Bosanski Novi, and KDZ605 relating to Bratunac. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that there is evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that persecutions charged as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 5(h) of the Statute were carried out by Bosnian Serb forces against Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats. In relation to Counts 4, 5, and 6, the accused does not raise any specific challenges with respect to municipalities. The Chamber has received evidence which suggests that Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats were killed by Bosnian Serb forces in the municipalities on a large scale in detention facilities, including as a result of cruel and inhumane treatment, and killings which occurred during and after the alleged take-over of these municipalities. This includes the testimony of Musan Talovic relating to Bratunac; Munira Selmanovic relating to Sokolac; Ahmet Zulic relating to Sanski Most; Eset Muracevic relating to Vogosca; KDZ041 relating to Novi Grad; and KDZ048 relating to Prijedor. The Chamber also received into evidence exhumation records as well as pathology and autopsy reports which provide evidence that Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats were killed in municipalities including in Rogatica, Sokolac, and Zvornik. The Chamber refers, for example, to P3276, P3297, P4106, and P4903. Having reviewed the evidence presented by the Prosecution, the Chamber finds that there is evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that murder charged as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 5(a) of the Statute and as a violation of the laws or customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute and specifically Common Article 3 and extermination charged as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 5(b) of the Statute were carried out by Bosnian Serb forces in the municipalities. In relation to Counts 7 and 8, the accused generally submits that there is no evidence of forcible transfer or deportation in the municipalities. The Chamber has heard evidence which suggests that a large number of Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats from the municipalities were intentionally forcibly displaced either within or across a de jure or de facto border by Bosnian Serb forces. This includes the evidence of KDZ605, Mehmed Music, KDZ024, KDZ026, and Selmanovic. The Chamber also received into evidence the report of Tabeau, who testified about refugees and displaced persons as well as changes to the ethnic composition in the municipalities. This is P4994. Having reviewed the evidence presented by the Prosecution, the Chamber therefore finds that there is evidence on which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that deportation charged as a crime against humanity punishable under Article 5(d) as well as forcible transfer, and inhumane act charged as a crime against humanity punishable under Article 5(i) of the Statute were carried out by Bosnian Serb forces in the municipalities. In relation to Count 1, the accused submits that there is no evidence upon which the Chamber could conclude that there was an intention to destroy the Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats. He further submits that displacement does not equate destruction and that the pattern of prisoner exchanges flies in the face of genocide as thousands of Bosnian Muslims were exchanged and released in 1992. The accused contends that the objective of the Bosnian Serb leadership to create a larger Serb state did not necessarily entail the destruction of the non-Serb population. In support, the accused refers to, inter alia, the 2007 judgement of the ICJ in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina against Serbia and Montenegro and several judgements of this Tribunal where genocide in the municipalities was found not to have been proven. He also refers to D2250, a chart prepared by Prosecution witness Tabeau reflecting the total numbers of dead and missing Bosnian Muslims from the seven municipalities where genocide is alleged to have occurred. The Prosecution responds that the fact that the desire to create a Serbian state may have had motives other than the commission of genocide is irrelevant. The Prosecution submits that what is of relevance is whether there was dolus specialis. In that respect, the Prosecution responds by reference to statements of the accused that he shared the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslim and/or Bosnian Croat groups in part and that he encouraged the destruction of this protected group by the organs under his authority and control. It further cites illustrative examples of incidents in Zvornik and Prijedor which, in the Prosecution's submission show genocidal intent. Finally, the Prosecution adds that there's no minimum numerical requirement for genocide and that displacement itself can contribute to destruction or can be evidence of genocidal intent. At the outset, the Chamber notes that the ICJ judgement and the Tribunal jurisprudence cited by the accused and the findings found therein in relation to the alleged genocide in municipalities in BiH are not binding in any way on the Chamber including for the purposes of its Rule 98 bis determination. Similarly, while the Prosecution correctly observes that no Chamber of the Tribunal referred to by the accused has entered a judgement for acquittal at the Rule 98 bis stage for genocide, this does not preclude this Chamber from reaching that conclusion on its review of the evidence before it. If the Chamber is convinced that taking the totality of the evidence presented by the Prosecution even at its highest there is no evidence on which it could convict the accused of genocide under Count 1, the Chamber should enter a judgement of acquittal for Count 1 at this stage. For the purposes of Count 1, the Prosecution alleges in the indictment that in some municipalities the alleged campaign of persecution between 31st March and 31st December 1992, "escalated to include conduct that manifested an intent to destroy in part the national, ethnical, and/or religious groups of Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats as such." The Chamber recalls that the alleged genocidal acts as charged in the indictment under Count 1 include: (1) killing of members of the protected group; (2) causing of serious bodily and mental harm to members of the protected group; and (3) detention under conditions of life calculated to bring about physical destruction of the protected group. The Chamber has reviewed evidence relating to the municipalities, including the testimony of Talovic from Bratunac; Sead Hodzic from Vlasenica; KDZ610 from Zvornik; KDZ239 from Foca; KDZ075 from Kljuc; and KDZ048 as well as Ivo Atlija from Prijedor. This and other evidence indicates that a large number of Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats were killed by Bosnian Serb forces in the municipalities during and after their alleged take-over and while in detention. As described earlier this evidence is capable of supporting a conclusion that Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats were killed on a large scale with the intent to kill with persecutory intent in relation to Counts 3 to 6 of the indictment. The Chamber notes that the determination of whether there is evidence capable of supporting a conviction for genocide does not involve a numerical assessment of the number of people killed and does not have a numeric threshold. However, the evidence the Chamber received in relation to the municipalities, even if taken at its highest, does not reach the level from which a reasonable trier of fact could infer that a significant section of the Bosnian Muslim and/or Bosnian Croat groups and a substantial number of members of these groups were targeted for destruction so as to have an impact on the existence of the Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats as such. As noted earlier, the Chamber recalls that the actus reus for genocide can also manifest itself by (1) causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group; or by (2) deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part. The Chamber recalls that serious bodily harm must go beyond temporary unhappiness, embarrassment or humiliation, and result in a grave and long-term disadvantage to a person's ability to lead a normal and constructive life, but it need not be permanent and irremediable. The Chamber has received evidence from witnesses including KDZ239 from Foca; KDZ050 and KDZ048 from Prijedor; KDZ605 from Bratunac; KDZ603 from Vlasenica; Jusuf Avdispahic from Zvornik; KDZ490 from Sanski Most, which indicates that Bosnian Serb forces caused serious bodily or mental harm to many Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats during their detention in multiple detention facilities. However, in order to support a conviction for genocide, the bodily or mental harm inflicted on members of a group must be of such a serious nature as to threaten its destruction in whole or in part. In that regard, the Chamber has not heard evidence, even taken at its highest, which could support a conclusion by a reasonable trier of fact that the harm caused reached a level where it contributed to or tended to contribute to the destruction of the Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats in whole or in part or that it was committed with the intent to destroy those groups. The Tribunal's jurisprudence establishes that forcible transfer does not constitute in and of itself a genocidal act, but where attended by such circumstances as to lead to the death of the whole or part of the displaced population, it may be considered an underlying offence that causes serious bodily or mental harm. The Chamber refers here to the Appeals Chamber's judgement in Krstic and the Trial Chamber's judgement in Popovic et al. The evidence heard by the Chamber indicates that the circumstances in which the Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats in the municipalities were forcibly transferred or displaced from their homes were attended by conditions of great hardship and suffering and that some of those displaced may have suffered serious bodily or mental harm during this process. However, the Chamber has not heard evidence which rises to the level which could sustain a conclusion that the serious bodily or mental harm suffered by those forcibly transferred in the municipalities was attended by such circumstances as to lead to the death of the whole or part of the displaced population for the purposes of the actus reus for genocide under Article 4(b) of the Statute. The evidence of the witnesses referred to earlier is also illustrative of the conditions of detention, including cruel and inhumane treatment, torture, physical and psychological abuse, rape and sexual violence, inhumane living conditions, forced labour, failure to provide adequate accommodation, shelter, food, water, medical care or hygienic facilities, in relation to which the Chamber already found there was sufficient evidence for the purpose of Count 3. However, in determining whether conditions of life imposed on the targeted group were calculated to bring about its physical destruction, the Chamber has to focus on the objective probability of these conditions leading to the physical destruction of the group in part and must assess factors like the nature of the conditions imposed, the length of time that members of the group were subjected to that, and characteristics of the targeted group such as vulnerability. When reviewing evidence going to Count 1 for the purpose of this ruling, the Chamber has indeed focussed on and assessed those factors. In addition, while doing so, the Chamber also reminded itself that the charge of deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part, does not require proof that the result was actually achieved. Having completed this review and analysis, the Chamber came to the conclusion that, for the purposes of Count 1, the evidence before it, even taken at its highest, cannot support the conclusion that the conditions of detention in the scheduled detention facilities reached a level which could support an inference that Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats were detained in conditions of life calculated to bring about their physical destruction. As mentioned earlier, the Chamber notes that in the absence of direct evidence that the physical perpetrators of the crimes alleged to have been committed in the municipalities carried out these crimes with genocidal intent, the Chamber can infer specific intent from a number of factors and circumstances, including the general context of the case, the means available to the perpetrator, the surrounding circumstances, the perpetration of other culpable acts systematically directed against the same group, the numerical scale of atrocities committed, the repetition of destructive and discriminatory acts, the derogatory language targeting the protected group, or the existence of a plan or policy to commit the underlying offence. As stated earlier, the Chamber has heard evidence of culpable acts systematically directed against Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats in the municipalities and of the repetition of discriminatory acts and derogatory language. However, the nature, scale, and context of these culpable acts, be it in all the municipalities covered by the indictment or the seven municipalities in which genocide is specifically alleged, do not reach the level from which a reasonable trier of fact could infer that they were committed with genocidal intent. Finally, having reviewed the totality of the evidence which the Chamber has received with respect to the killing, of serious bodily or mental harm to, the forcible displacement of, and conditions of life inflicted on Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats in detention facilities in the municipalities, the Chamber finds that there is no evidence that these actions reached a level from which a reasonable trier of fact could draw an inference that they were committed with an intent to destroy in whole or in part the Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats as such. As stated earlier, the Prosecution in its response to the accused also refers to evidence of statements and speeches made by him and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership which, according to the Prosecution, contained rhetorical warning of the disappearance, elimination, annihilation or extinction of Bosnian Muslims in the event that war broke out. The Chamber has considered these examples as well as the other evidence received in relation to the accused in light of the scale and the context of the alleged crimes in the municipalities in 1992, and the inability to infer genocidal intent from other factors. Following this review, the Chamber finds that notwithstanding the statements of the accused, there is no evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could find that the acts of killing, serious bodily or mental harm, and conditions of life inflicted on the Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats were perpetrated with the dolus specialis required for genocide. Having reviewed the evidence admitted in this case with respect to Count 1, the Chamber finds that there is no evidence, even taken at its highest, which could be capable of supporting a conviction for genocide in the municipalities as charged under Article 4(3) of the Statute. In relation to his responsibility with regard to the municipalities component of the case, the accused submits that there is no evidence that Bosnian Serb leadership intended to permanently remove the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the territories in BiH referred to in the indictment. He also submits that there is no evidence that there was a take-over of power in the municipalities or that incident happened at the initiative of the Serbs or there was a systematic approach to the question of minorities in the Republika Srpska from which the crimes charged in the indictment would result. Finally, in relation to the detention facilities in the municipalities, he submits that it was difficult as president to influence what was happening on the ground because he had neither communication nor access. The Prosecution, inter alia, responds that there is evidence that the accused sought an ethnically clean state and that the redistribution of the population was to take place over a vast amount of territory. The Prosecution also contends that the accused was receiving information on the mistreatment in the detention facilities and undertook efforts to distance himself from them. First, the Chamber notes that there is evidence that throughout the period of the indictment, members of the Bosnian Serb leadership met often, co-ordinated, and exchanged information as well as ideas. The Chamber has received in evidence the records of hundreds of regular meetings attended by the Bosnian Serb leadership between 1991 and 1995, sometimes with municipal or regional leaders and members of the VRS Main Staff, during which the participants discussed strategy and policies and often espoused the same goals and shared similar rhetoric. The Chamber also refers to the hundreds of intercepted conversations admitted into evidence, as well as to the testimony of Wilson. Second, contrary to what the accused asserts, there is evidence of a planned take-over of power in the municipalities which sought to establish separate Bosnian Serb institutions and to create a Bosnian Serb homogeneous state for which the Bosnian Serbs were actively preparing. The Chamber refers to P960, P2548, P2552, P2581, and P3337. The Chamber received ample evidence that throughout the conflict the objective of an ethnically homogeneous territory was reiterated by Bosnian Serb leadership. The Chamber refers, for example, to P1385, P2556, D86, and D90. Finally, the Chamber heard evidence that throughout the municipalities, the policy of the Bosnian Serb leadership did result in what Harland described as huge-scale violent expulsion of non-Serb population. Accordingly, there is evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that during the period relevant to the indictment there existed a joint criminal enterprise composed of, inter alia, members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including the accused the purpose of which was to permanently remove the Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats from Bosnian-Serb claimed territories in BiH. In relation to his responsibility for the municipalities component of the case, the accused does not make a specific challenge since he is challenging the very existence of a joint criminal enterprise. First, there is evidence that as charged in paragraph 14 of the indictment, the accused as president of the SDS and later Republika Srpska president formulated and promoted the development and implementation of SDS and Bosnian Serb governmental policies intended to advance the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. The Chamber refers in particular to the evidence in relation to the promulgation of the six strategic goals and their implementation on the ground through a number of VRS directives for military operations. This is in P161, P976, P3036, and D325. The Chamber also received evidence that the accused disseminated and encouraged the dissemination of propaganda to Bosnian Serbs intended to engender fear and hatred of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats in Bosnian Serbs. The Chamber received evidence that within its unit the Main Staff accentuated the message that the Bosnian Serbs were threatened by aggression and genocide and instructed units to "take care to achieve the desired information and propaganda effects." The Chamber refers, for example, to P962, D270, and D325. Okun testified that in negotiations with international representatives, the accused "never denied Serb ambitions for a separate republic in Bosnia nor that his forces had conducted 'ethnic cleansing' or military operations again the other Bosnian nationalities. Rather, he attempted to justify the actions of the people he claimed to represent," namely that "they the Serb people had to be protected from the aggressiveness of the Muslims or the Turks." There is also evidence that the accused directed and encouraged Bosnian Serb political and governmental organs and Bosnian Serb forces to carry out acts in furtherance of the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. The Chamber refers to the evidence that the accused encouraged municipal leaders to undertake actions to create a homogeneous territory. This is in P3405 and D92. Contrary to the accused's submission in relation to his lack of influence on and information as to the events on the ground, the Chamber received evidence that the accused failed, while under a duty to do so, to take adequate steps to ensure that Bosnian Serb political and governmental organs and Bosnian Serb forces would act to protect Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats residing in areas under their control. For instance, there is evidence that as early as 1992, there were working communications systems from the Supreme Commander to the lower levels, and therefore that there were mechanisms through which the accused was informed regularly and in detail of the situation on the ground. The Chamber refers to D325. Of relevance to the accused's knowledge of existence of detention facilities in Prijedor, the Chamber refers to the testimony of Wilson and of Edward Vulliamy. Vulliamy testified that the accused told him that he could order that the Omarska detention facility be closed down in two days and that he knew the prisoners at Omarska did not have enough food. The Chamber also heard evidence that Milorad Davidovic attended a meeting with the accused and Mladic, during which the accused assured Davidovic that measures to prevent looting were already taken and that further attempts to prevent looting would be made, but instructed that no arrests of Serbs should be made to avoid conflicts between Serbs. The accused said "that it was very important for Serbs not to fight one another as it had been the case in some other conflicts, such as during the Second World War, even if it is done at the expenses of not punishing perpetrators of crimes." Accordingly, the Chamber is satisfied that there is evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that during the period relevant to the indictment, through his acts and omissions, the accused voluntarily participated in a joint criminal enterprise composed of, inter alia, members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, the purpose of which was to permanently remove the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from Bosnian-Serb claimed territory in BiH, that he shared the intent of the other members of this joint criminal enterprise to carry out its objective through the commission of the crimes of persecutions, extermination, murder, deportation and forcible transfer as inhumane acts, and that he contributed to it through his acts and omissions. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber partially grants the accused's motion under Rule 98 bis of the Rules, enters a judgement of acquittal on Count 1 of the indictment, and dismisses the remainder of the motion. That was the ruling, and I'd like to deal with, in private session briefly, a couple of matters. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The hearing is now adjourned until the 3rd of September, 2012, when we will have a Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of September, 2012. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.07 p.m.,
